---
name: h3-gemm-screen-recipe
description: How to screen a dit_gemm.comp build on H3's real shapes with clocks and a bit-identical gate (H3_GEMM_SPV/WAVE/KRANGE_SPV/REF), ~2.5 min a run.
metadata:
  type: project
---

The fastest honest GEMM screen in the repo (KERNELS.md G1/G2, 2026-09-29): compile the arm with glslc to the scratchpad, then from `h3/dit`:

```
H3_SHAPES=480 H3_PROFILE=1 H3_BANK=q8 H3_GEMM_SPV=$S/arm.spv [H3_GEMM_WAVE=32] \
  [H3_GEMM_KRANGE_SPV=$S/arm_krange.spv] H3_GEMM_REF=$S/ref480.bits \
  ./dit.test -test.run TestGPUShapes -test.v -test.timeout 20m
```

with a 100 ms sampler on `/sys/class/hwmon/hwmon2/{freq1_input,power1_average}` running beside it (mode/percentiles over samples ≥125 W = the forward). ~2.5 min a run (42 GB staging via bank-cache, two 480p forwards). The first `H3_GEMM_REF` run writes the velocities' bits, every later one compares: a scheduling arm must be bit-identical. Builds that are wrong by construction (`L0_LOADS`, `STAGE_L0`) are still timed. Build the test binary once (`go test -c -o $S/dit.test ./h3/dit`) and never edit shaders during a sweep.

**Why:** the suite (`cmd/bench`) doesn't see the real M/N/K, the clock under a real forward (~2620–2680 MHz at the 154 W cap), or the MALL-overflowing down projection; the pipeline screen does, and G2's whole ladder ran on it.

**How to apply:** use it for any `dit_gemm.comp` arm; the `wave` field on H3's GEMM variant table is how wave32 is pinned. Related: [[coopmat-fragments-cost-8-vgprs]], [[never-edit-source-during-a-sweep]], [[a-benchmark-that-gets-faster]].

Three compiler/hardware facts about cooperative matrices on this part (Mesa 26.2.2 RADV, RDNA3.5), established in KERNELS.md G2 / research §2.9 (2026-09-29):

- A 16x16 fp16 A or B fragment is **8 VGPRs at wave64 and at wave32** (the hardware replicates it across the 16-lane groups: 4x at wave64, 2x at wave32), and a fragment load moves 4x (2x) its 512 B through L0→VGPR. The accumulator is 4 VGPRs at wave64, 8 at wave32.
- **ACO cannot coalesce a coopmat carried across a loop back-edge**: it copies it as ~16 `v_mov_b16`. Any register double-buffering / software pipelining of fragments across K tiles compiles to hundreds of moves a trip and loses. Only shapes that carry nothing (a hoisted multi-tile slab, or LDS staging) measure a prefetch.
- `coopMatLoad` from `shared` lowers to four `ds_load_b64` per fragment, for which the LDS serves 16 lanes a clock: the conflict-free row/column pitch is 36 halves (18 dwords), not 24 (16-lane 2-way) and not 16 (4-way).

**Why:** §6.5 planned a "+24 VGPR" register prefetch that was really +96 and then un-coalescable; two arms were dead before they ran. The shipped GEMM (`dit_gemm_wg128x256_lds_w32`) is LDS-staged slabs at wave32 because of exactly these three facts.

**How to apply:** don't build cross-iteration register pipelines of coopmat operands on this Mesa; read `RADV_DEBUG=asm` for `v_mov_b16` counts before timing any loop that carries fragments; LDS fragment pitches are 36 halves. See [[strix-halo-bench-runs]] and [[h3-gemm-screen-recipe]].

The fastest honest GEMM screen in the repo (KERNELS.md G1/G2, 2026-09-29): compile the arm with glslc to the scratchpad, then from `h3/dit`:

```
H3_SHAPES=480 H3_PROFILE=1 H3_BANK=q8 H3_GEMM_SPV=$S/arm.spv [H3_GEMM_WAVE=32] \
  [H3_GEMM_KRANGE_SPV=$S/arm_krange.spv] H3_GEMM_REF=$S/ref480.bits \
  ./dit.test -test.run TestGPUShapes -test.v -test.timeout 20m
```

with a 100 ms sampler on `/sys/class/hwmon/hwmon2/{freq1_input,power1_average}` running beside it (mode/percentiles over samples ≥125 W = the forward). ~2.5 min a run (42 GB staging via bank-cache, two 480p forwards). The first `H3_GEMM_REF` run writes the velocities' bits, every later one compares: a scheduling arm must be bit-identical. Builds that are wrong by construction (`L0_LOADS`, `STAGE_L0`) are still timed. Build the test binary once (`go test -c -o $S/dit.test ./h3/dit`) and never edit shaders during a sweep.

**Why:** the suite (`cmd/bench`) doesn't see the real M/N/K, the clock under a real forward (~2620–2680 MHz at the 154 W cap), or the MALL-overflowing down projection; the pipeline screen does, and G2's whole ladder ran on it.

**How to apply:** use it for any `dit_gemm.comp` arm; the `wave` field on H3's GEMM variant table is how wave32 is pinned. Related: [[coopmat-fragments-cost-8-vgprs]], [[never-edit-source-during-a-sweep]], [[a-benchmark-that-gets-faster]].

Root `KERNELS.md` (opened 2026-09-29, G-stages) is the live plan for taking the WMMA kernels from 42.0 toward 55.5 TFLOP/s. Facts a session needs before touching it: the suite's best GEMM ran at 2813 MHz / 137 W where the `peak` probe ran 2899 / 110, so utilisation is quoted per clock (478 FLOP/clk/CU is the measured peak); the shipped `dit_gemm_wg128x256_bt16_swz8` is 240 VGPRs, no spill, `BK_TILES 1`, no prefetch; both head-128 attentions spill 112–126 VGPRs. `cmd/probe` (RADV_DEBUG=shaderstats/asm) was deleted by accident on 2026-09-22 and restored 2026-09-29.

G0/G1 (2026-09-29, research §0.6, §6.5): **no real kernel runs at 2899 MHz.** A video forward runs at 2600–2650 MHz and ~149 W (package-limited ~150 W), so its ceiling is 49.9 TFLOP/s, not 55.5; a 20 ms bench burst sees 2813. **32 busy CPU threads halve the GPU clock** and make a forward 1.67x slower: never run a CPU-heavy job (staging, audio decode, a test sweep) beside a device timing, and sample `hwmon/freq1_input` + `power1_average` around any in-pipeline number. The shipped GEMM's rate is flat from 1 to 3+ workgroups a CU, and ACO does not prefetch across K tiles.

**Why:** eight verticals ended on "the GEMMs are at their ceiling" without the ceiling ever being pushed; a GEMM win lands in every served request.

**How to apply:** file a closed finding under the next free `§N.M` in `research/` and point the G-stage at it; prove a lever in `gemm_wmma.comp`'s suite first, ship it in `dit_gemm.comp`, and screen it with each vertical's own tool ([[strix-halo-bench-runs]], [[never-edit-source-during-a-sweep]]).

That blank line predates my edit (it sits in the Kev section), so I'll leave the file as is rather than reformat another session's region. Work is complete; here is the recap.

**G2 is done and shipped for H3.** The next item in KERNELS.md was the register-prefetch GEMM. The prefetch that actually fits is not registers but LDS at wave32: the new `dit_gemm_wg128x256_lds_w32` build (plus its KRANGE companion) stages each K slab through 24 staging registers into a double-buffered LDS plane a slab ahead, with eight wave32 waves of 4×4 tiles in the same 128×256 workgroup. It is bit-identical to the wave64 kernel it replaces.

| 480p H3 forward, int8 | qkv | gate / up | o | down | forward | per clock |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| wave64 4×8 (was shipped) | 37.2 | 37.3 / 37.1 | 35.4 | 28.7 | 29.86 s | 74% |
| `lds_w32`, two runs | 41.1 / 40.9 | 40.7 / 40.7 | 38.9 / 39.1 | 40.8 / 40.6 | 27.16 / 27.11 s | 80% |

Gates passed: the `H3_GEMM_REF` bit-identical comparison against the old build's velocities on every arm, and `TestGPUForward` on the shipped build (all blocks and the forward inside their bounds, the down split bit-identical).

**What decided it, from a twelve-rung ladder** (all in `research/2.9-lds-staged-wave32-gemm.md`):
- A wave64 fragment is 8 VGPRs, not 2, because the hardware replicates it four times across the lane groups. G1's "+24 VGPRs" for a prefetched tile was really +96.
- ACO cannot carry a cooperative-matrix fragment across a loop back-edge without copying it element by element, so both register-pipelining arms compiled to hundreds of `v_mov_b16` a trip and lost before measuring anything.
- Wave32 halves the bytes a fragment read moves but caps the tile at 4×4; fed from global memory it runs at 21.5 TFLOP/s, fed from LDS at 40.9. LDS fragment reads lower to `ds_load_b64`, so the conflict-free pitch is 36 halves, and §2.1's old LDS loss was an unpadded 4-way conflict, not the mechanism.
- Refused: strength-reduced addresses (nothing), four hoisted tiles, the read order inside a slab, LDS pitches 16 and 24.

**Files changed:** `shaders/dit_gemm.comp` (the `SR`, `PIPE`, `DB`, `LDS_STAGE`, `STAGE_L0`, `LOAD_ORDER` arms, documented with verdicts), `shaders/shaders.go` (two builds), `h3/dit/gpu.go` (a `wave` field on the GEMM variants, big and KRANGE pinned to wave32), `h3/dit/gpu_test.go` (`H3_GEMM_WAVE`, `H3_GEMM_KRANGE_SPV`, `H3_GEMM_REF`), plus KERNELS.md, VIDEO.md M11, TODO.md, `research/README.md` and two memory notes. Nothing is committed; the auto-committer owns main.

**What's next:** G8 carry-in. Eight other hosts still create the wave64 kernel (`zimage/qwen`, `qimage/dit`, `parakeet`, `h3/vae`, `kev`, `ocr`, `ace/dit`, `ace/lm`); each needs its pipeline pinned to wave32, K checked as a multiple of 32, and its own screen re-run. The served binary also needs a redeploy to pick up the H3 change. The remaining ~18 points are the LDS-side schedule inside a slab, filed as G-o8.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). ---
name: lds-gemm-needs-a-full-machine
description: The shipped LDS-staged wave32 GEMM loses to the old wave64 build below ~40 workgroups (~1000 rows at N 2560); which hosts guard it and how.
metadata:
  type: project
---

`dit_gemm_wg128x256_lds_w32` (KERNELS.md G2/G8, 2026-09-29) wins 5–16% wherever the grid fills the 40 CUs, and **loses 8–11% under ~40 workgroups** (rows × N / 32,768): ACE's 30 s clip at 375 rows is 130 vs 120 ms a forward on the wave64 build; parakeet's rung at 138–768 frames loses too. The per-slab barrier and staging are the cost at low occupancy.

Guards in the tree: `ace/dit` keeps the wave64 build as `gemmBigW64` and switches at `bigW64Rows = 1024`; kev/ocr/ace-lm/zimage/parakeet ladders already schedule smaller rungs below ~192 rows or (parakeet) never pick the big rung. `h3/vae` had K = H + 16 (a bias column) and now rounds K to `gemmVariants[gemmBig].bk` (32).

**Why:** a screen on H3's 15,936-row shapes said +10%; the carry-in found the small-M loss only because every host was re-screened on its own shapes.

**How to apply:** any new host of the big GEMM must screen its short inputs against the wave64 build (`shaders.DiTGEMMWG128x256TiledSWZ8`, wave 0) before defaulting to the LDS one; keep both in the variant table. See [[coopmat-fragments-cost-8-vgprs]], [[h3-gemm-screen-recipe]].

`dit_gemm_wg128x256_lds_w32` (KERNELS.md G2/G8, 2026-09-29) wins 5–16% wherever the grid fills the 40 CUs, and **loses 8–11% under ~40 workgroups** (rows × N / 32,768): ACE's 30 s clip at 375 rows is 130 vs 120 ms a forward on the wave64 build; parakeet's rung at 138–768 frames loses too. The per-slab barrier and staging are the cost at low occupancy.

Guards in the tree: `ace/dit` keeps the wave64 build as `gemmBigW64` and switches at `bigW64Rows = 1024`; kev/ocr/ace-lm/zimage/parakeet ladders already schedule smaller rungs below ~192 rows or (parakeet) never pick the big rung. `h3/vae` had K = H + 16 (a bias column) and now rounds K to `gemmVariants[gemmBig].bk` (32).

**Why:** a screen on H3's 15,936-row shapes said +10%; the carry-in found the small-M loss only because every host was re-screened on its own shapes.

**How to apply:** any new host of the big GEMM must screen its short inputs against the wave64 build (`shaders.DiTGEMMWG128x256TiledSWZ8`, wave 0) before defaulting to the LDS one; keep both in the variant table. See [[coopmat-fragments-cost-8-vgprs]], [[h3-gemm-screen-recipe]].

**G8 carry-in is complete.** All nine hosts of the 128×256 GEMM now create the wave32 LDS-staged build, pinned through a `wave` field on each variant table, and every host's own gate passes.

| host | gate | screen (same session, old → new) |
|---|---|---|
| h3/dit | bit-identical forward | 480p forward 29.86 → 27.11 s |
| h3/vae | PSNR 81.7 dB unchanged | 480p decode 37.1 → 35.5 s |
| qimage/dit | 1024² oracle | step 2179 → 2058 ms (−5.6%), the five-arm screen |
| ace/dit | teacher-forced DiT | 8 forwards at 30 s / 2 / 4 / 10 min: 0.96 / 3.27 / 6.76 / 18.79 s |
| kev (fp16 bank) | row match | 494-token pass 154 → 132 ms |
| parakeet | encoder stack | its plan never picks the rung; the rung itself loses at ≤768 frames |
| zimage/qwen | encoder + kernels agree | no timing screen |
| ocr | six cases token-identical | page prefill 100 → 102 ms |
| ace/lm | logits + determinism | 239-row prefill 106 ms |

**Two things the carry-in found that the H3 screen could not:**
- The build needs a full machine. Under ~40 workgroups (about 1000 rows at N = 2560) the per-slab barrier shows and it loses 8–11% to the old wave64 build. ACE's 30 s clip was 130 against 120 ms a forward, so `ace/dit` keeps both builds and switches at 1024 rows (`bigW64Rows`); the 64×64 rung was never the answer. The other short-input hosts already schedule smaller rungs.
- The VAE's bias column made K = H + 16. Its K now rounds up to the big GEMM's 32-wide tile, with zero pad columns in both operands, and the decode is unchanged at 81.7 dB.

**Records:** KERNELS.md has the G8 table and a session-4 handoff, the §2.9 file its carry-in paragraph, VIDEO.md the VAE decode, and three memory notes cover the compiler facts, the screen recipe and the small-M rule. Tree builds, vets and is formatted; nothing committed, the auto-committer owns main. The served binary still needs a redeploy to pick any of this up.

**Next candidates:** G-o8 (the remaining ~18 points are the LDS-side schedule inside a slab), G4 (attention, whose head-128 builds spill), or G5 (int8 in registers; Kev's fp16 rung now beats its served int8 rung at 494 tokens, which says that is where the LDS round trip still costs).
